message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This bid is unusual in that it is not based on assumptions about demand: we tested the exact opening pattern at Ashgrove before asking for a penny, and measured the results hour by hour. The pilot showed strong uptake, with evening visits running close to daytime levels and Sunday sessions very popular with families, and new memberships up by about two-thirds on the year before. That gives Members real local evidence that the hours will be used. The costing is equally careful. Staffing is built up from first principles, hours times staff times weeks times branches at the correct graded rate with on-costs, and utilities are taken from actual pilot spend rather than estimates, all of which sums to £174,000. We also looked seriously at the cheaper self-service alternative and explain why it would cost more once building works are included. I am confident this is a well-tested, carefully costed proposal that delivers on the Council Plan.
</author>

<document>
Budget Justification: Extended Opening Hours at Five Branch Libraries, 2027-28
Library Services, Westmoor Borough Council, September 2026

1. Request
Library Services requests a growth bid of £174,000 in the 2027-28 revenue budget to extend opening hours at five branch libraries (Ashgrove, Fenwick, Holt Lane, Kingsmead and Millbrook) by ten hours a week each, from 38 to 48 hours.

2. Rationale
The five branches currently close at 5 pm on weekdays and do not open on Sundays. Residents' surveys have repeatedly identified opening hours as the main barrier to library use among working-age adults: in the 2025 Residents' Survey, 44% of non-users aged 25-54 said the library "is never open when I can go". The Council Plan commits to increasing library use among working-age residents and to supporting adult learning and job-seeking.

Each branch would add late opening until 8 pm on Tuesdays and Thursdays (six additional hours) and Sunday opening from 11 am to 3 pm (four additional hours).

3. Evidence from the Ashgrove pilot
From October 2025 to March 2026, Ashgrove trialled exactly this pattern, funded from one-off underspends.

Table 1. Ashgrove pilot: average visits per opening hour, October 2025 to March 2026
Time slot | Visits per hour
Weekday 9 am - 12 pm | 46
Weekday 12 pm - 5 pm | 58
Tuesday and Thursday 5 pm - 8 pm (new) | 21
Saturday 9 am - 1 pm | 64
Sunday 11 am - 3 pm (new) | 52

Over the pilot, Ashgrove recorded 1,140 new library memberships, compared with 690 in the same months a year earlier. Sunday sessions were particularly popular with families, and a weekly job club in the Thursday evening slot was fully booked from its third week.

Evening visits at Ashgrove averaged close to the weekday daytime level, which shows that there is strong latent demand for evening opening and that the new hours will be well used across all five branches.

4. Costs
Additional hours need two staff on duty at all times, in line with the Council's lone-working policy. Staffing is calculated on 50 weeks a year, allowing for bank holiday closures.

Table 2. Cost of extended hours, five branches
Item | Basis | Cost
Staffing | 10 hours x 2 staff x 50 weeks x 5 branches = 5,000 hours at £24.80 per hour (including on-costs) | £124,000
Utilities and caretaking | £6,500 per branch | £32,500
Self-service kiosk upgrades (maintenance contract) | 5 branches | £7,500
Total | | £174,000

The staffing rate is the mid-point of the Library Assistant grade plus 28% on-costs and an enhancement for Sunday working. Utilities and caretaking costs are based on the actual additional costs recorded at Ashgrove during the pilot, scaled to a full year.

5. Value for money
At current visit rates, the extra hours across the five branches would generate roughly 84,000 additional visits a year, at a cost of around £2 per visit. This compares favourably with the borough's average cost per library visit of £3.40.

6. Alternatives considered
We considered opening the branches with self-service access only in the extra hours, as some authorities have done. This would cut staffing costs by around two-thirds, but the Council's insurers have advised that unstaffed opening would require building alterations and CCTV at an estimated £60,000 per branch, and it would not support the job club and family activities that drove much of the pilot's success.

7. Risks
Recruitment. We expect to fill most additional hours from existing part-time staff who have asked for more hours, as happened during the pilot.
Demand at other branches. Ashgrove is our busiest branch, and demand at the other four may be lower. We will review usage after six months.

8. Conclusion
The twelve-month Ashgrove pilot has demonstrated strong demand for evening and Sunday opening, with new memberships up by two-thirds and evening use close to daytime levels. We ask Members to approve a growth bid of £174,000 to extend this successful model to all five branches from April 2027.
</document>
response:
# Review: Extended Opening Hours Budget Justification

The proposal has a real strength: an actual pilot of the exact pattern being proposed, which is better evidence than most growth bids have. But the document has an arithmetic error in the total, contradicts itself on the length of the pilot, and draws conclusions from the pilot data that the data don't support. The author's description repeats several of these problems and adds a claim about the self-service option that the document doesn't make.

## 1. The cost table doesn't add up to £174,000

| Item | Cost |
|---|---|
| Staffing | £124,000 |
| Utilities and caretaking | £32,500 |
| Kiosk maintenance | £7,500 |
| **Actual sum** | **£164,000** |

The individual lines are calculated correctly: 5,000 hours × £24.80 = £124,000, and £6,500 × 5 = £32,500. The **total is overstated by £10,000**. Either a cost line is missing or the total is wrong. This has to be resolved before the bid goes to Members, because the £174,000 figure is used in the request, the value-for-money section, the conclusion and the author's summary.

It's also unclear why a **self-service kiosk maintenance contract** belongs in a bid for *staffed* extended hours. It should be explained or removed.

## 2. The pilot was six months, not twelve

Section 3 says the pilot ran **October 2025 to March 2026**, which is six months. Section 8 calls it "the twelve-month Ashgrove pilot." Members will notice this. It also matters for interpreting the results: the pilot covered only autumn and winter, so there are no spring or summer data, when evening demand may be quite different.

## 3. Evening use is not "close to daytime levels"

Table 1 contradicts this claim, which appears in both the document and the author's summary:

| Slot | Visits/hour | Compared with weekday daytime |
|---|---|---|
| Weekday daytime | 46–58 | — |
| **Tue/Thu evening (new)** | **21** | **≈36–46%** |
| Sunday (new) | 52 | ≈90–113% |

**Sunday** opening is the strong result. Evening use is less than half of daytime use. The document then goes further than its own data, saying evening use "shows that… the new hours will be well used **across all five branches**," even though section 7 concedes that Ashgrove is the busiest branch.

Splitting the cost by slot, using the document's own figures, makes the difference clear:

| | Hours/yr (5 branches) | Est. visits | Approx. cost | Cost per visit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evenings | 1,500 | 31,500 | ≈£94,000 | **≈£3.00** |
| Sundays | 1,000 | 52,000 | ≈£63,000 | **≈£1.20** |

The figures assume costs split 60/40 in proportion to hours, with Sunday enhancement ignored.

At Ashgrove's rates, evening opening already costs about the same per visit as the borough average of £3.40. At less busy branches it would cost more. Members may reasonably ask whether to fund Sundays now and evenings more selectively.

## 4. The pilot evidence is weaker than presented

- **No baseline for total visits.** The table shows use of the new hours but not whether total visits to Ashgrove rose. Some evening and Sunday visitors may simply have moved from existing hours. The useful figure is total visits during the pilot compared with the same months a year earlier.
- **The membership increase can't be attributed to the new hours.** 1,140 against 690 is a rise of about 65%, so "about two-thirds" is correct as arithmetic. But it's a simple before-and-after comparison: it covers joiners at all hours, with no breakdown by hour and no comparison with other branches over the same period. If other branches also saw rising membership, the effect is smaller than claimed.
- **Target group not measured.** The rationale is about **working-age non-users**. The pilot reports families on Sundays and a full job club, but no data on visitors' age or whether they were previously non-users. The link to the Council Plan objective is assumed, not shown.
- **Job club capacity.** "Fully booked from week three" means little without the number of places.

## 5. Visit projection and value for money

- The 84,000 figure checks out. Per branch per week there are 6 hours × 21 + 4 hours × 52 = 334 visits; × 50 weeks × 5 branches = 83,500. But it applies **Ashgrove's rates to all five branches**, which section 7 itself says is likely to overstate demand.
- £174,000 ÷ 84,000 ≈ £2.07 per visit, which is correct on the stated total (£1.95 on the corrected £164,000). But it compares a **marginal** cost with the borough's **average** cost, which includes buildings, stock and management. That's not like-for-like and flatters the proposal.
- A **sensitivity case** would help, for example cost per visit if the other four branches reach 60% of Ashgrove's use.

## 6. Costing points

- **Utilities:** The figure is "actual pilot spend… scaled to a full year." It's a winter-only extrapolation from a single building, not simply "actual spend" as the author describes it. It probably *overstates* heating and lighting, which is a prudent error, but that should be stated. The other buildings may differ.
- **Staffing:** The structure and arithmetic are sound. A single blended rate including the Sunday enhancement is acceptable, but showing evening and Sunday rates separately would make the figure verifiable.

## 7. The self-service comparison is presented unfairly

The author says self-service "would cost more once building works are included." The document doesn't actually claim that, and its own numbers don't support it over any reasonable period:

- Staffing saving: about two-thirds of £124,000, roughly **£83,000 a year**.
- Building works: £60,000 × 5 = **£300,000 one-off**, which is capital rather than revenue.
- **Break-even is about 3.6 years.** After that, self-service is cheaper every year.

There may be good reasons to prefer staffed opening: the job club, family activities, the insurers' conditions. These should be argued on their merits, with the capital/revenue split and the payback period shown honestly. A **hybrid** should also be considered, for example staffed Sundays and the Thursday job-club evening, with self-service or no opening on Tuesday evenings.

## 8. Risks

- **Usage review:** "Review usage after six months" needs criteria. What usage level at a given branch would lead to the hours being reduced?
- **Recruitment:** Relying on existing part-time staff is reasonable given the pilot. It's worth confirming that enough hours are available across all five branches, not just Ashgrove.

## Author's description compared with the document

| Author's claim | What the document supports |
|---|---|
| Evening visits "close to daytime levels" | 21/hr vs 46–58/hr, under half |
| Memberships up about two-thirds | Correct (+65%), but not attributable to the new hours |
| Costs sum to £174,000 | Lines sum to £164,000 |
| Utilities from "actual pilot spend" | Six winter months at one branch, extrapolated |
| Self-service "would cost more" | Not claimed in the document; cheaper after about 3.6 years |
| (Document) "twelve-month pilot" | Six months |

## Recommendations

1. Fix the total (£164,000 or identify the missing £10,000), and explain or remove the kiosk line.
2. Correct "twelve-month" to six months.
3. Rewrite the evidence section to say that Sunday demand is strong and evening demand moderate, and drop "close to daytime levels."
4. Add total-visit and membership comparisons, ideally against the other branches as a control.
5. Show cost per visit separately for evenings and Sundays, with a lower-demand case for the other four branches.
6. Present the self-service option fairly, including the capital/revenue split, break-even, and a hybrid option.
7. Set review criteria for the six-month usage check.

The Sunday case looks strong, and the pilot is a real asset. With these corrections the bid would be more credible to Members, even if the headline claims become more modest.
